## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

**Before entering plan mode:** if you haven't already brainstormed, invoke the brainstorming skill first.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |

| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

    Every byte a tool returns enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session.     1. GATHER: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute(commands, queries)
       - Primary research tool. Runs commands in parallel, auto-indexes each output, and (when queries are passed) returns matching sections in the same round trip — no follow-up search call.
       - Each command: {label: "section header", command: "shell command"}; the label becomes the FTS5 chunk title — descriptive labels improve search.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

name: education-planner
description: Plans the Applied Performance staff education program — finds content gaps by comparing the question ledger against delivered sessions, sequences the 5-Slides-in-5-Minutes series, and specs each deck before handing off to the five-slides-generator skill. tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob

### AgentAssist education-planner agent > Deck spec
## Deck spec

Before handing to `five-slides-generator`, produce:

```
TOPIC
AUDIENCE            one, named
LEDGER ORIGIN       Q-numbers this answers (or: none — proactive)
COMPETENCY DOMAIN   code + the level this moves people to
PREREQUISITES       what they must already have; if unmet, teach that first

THE ONE THING       the single sentence they should still know in a month.
                    If you cannot write it, the topic is not ready.
THE MISCONCEPTION   what they currently believe that is wrong. Every good
                    session corrects something, not just adds something.

SLIDE ARC           1. the hook — why they should care, in their terms
                    2-4. the substance
                    5. the so-what — what changes Monday
SO-WHAT             the concrete behavior change requested
ANTICIPATED PUSHBACK   the two hardest questions, and honest answers —
                    including "we don't know" where that is the truth
```

**Every deck must correct a misconception.** Additive-only sessions are forgotten by
Friday. The ones that stick are the ones that told someone their mental model was
wrong and showed them why.

description: "Generate a '5 Slides in 5 Minutes' PowerPoint deck for Baylor Athletics Applied Performance — research, narrative, pptxgenjs, .pptx build, QA. Use whenever the user mentions '5 slides,' '5 slides in 5 minutes,' or gives a topic they want a Performance School deck on. # 5 Slides in 5 Minutes Generator

Generates polished, on-brand PowerPoint decks for Baylor Athletics' Applied Performance "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" Performance School education series. Each deck is a 5-minute cross-functional staff presentation that surfaces one topic, delivers a key insight, and sparks deeper conversation.

**Read [`references/code-template.md`](references/code-template.md) before writing any pptxgenjs code.** It contains the full structural template, design system constants, and common pitfalls.

**Read [`references/topic-library.md`](references/topic-library.md)** to understand the 40-topic library context when a topic is named.

**Read [`references/talking-points.md`](references/talking-points.md)** when generating speaker notes or when the user asks for a presenter version. Covers per-slide timing budget (~4:45 total) and talking-point structure.

**Read [`references/marp-template.md`](references/marp-template.md)** when the user asks for a "Marp version", "markdown slides", ".md version of the deck", or any version-controllable / shareable format alongside the pptx. Generates a second `.md` output mirroring the pptx narrative.

---

## The 5-Slide Narrative Structure

Every deck follows this fixed 5-slide arc, always in this order:

| Slide | Name | Purpose | Background |
|-------|------|---------|------------|
| 1 | Hook | Grab attention, frame the question | DARK |
| 2 | Problem / Context | Show the gap, the stakes, or the misunderstanding | LIGHT |
| 3 | Insight | The core scientific or practical concept | DARK |
| 4 | Application | What this looks like in practice for this audience | LIGHT |
| 5 | Takeaway | One clear point + a discussion question | DARK |

Dark/light alternation is a visual signature of the series. Never break this pattern.

---

## Full Workflow

### Step 1: Confirm the Topic

If the user gave a topic, proceed. If ambiguous, ask one clarifying question: "What's the core question you want answered in 5 minutes?"

### Step 2: Research the Content

Use WebSearch (or the firecrawl-search skill for full-page content) to gather 4-6 factual data points, statistics, or key findings on the topic. Prioritize:
- Peer-reviewed research findings
- Clinical or applied sport science data
- Practical frameworks used by elite programs

Take note of actual numbers and sources. Every stat in the deck must come from research, not fabrication.

### Step 3: Plan the Narrative

Before writing any code, draft the 5-slide narrative outline in the chat:

```
Slide 1 Hook:    [Provocative question or surprising stat]
Slide 2 Context: [The gap, problem, or misconception]
Slide 3 Insight: [The mechanism or framework]
Slide 4 Apply:   [Concrete example for the H&W team]
```

# Module map

> **Draft v1 — 2026-08-18.** Reading assignments are now filled from the **real** CPSS
> chapter list (31 chapters across 7 Parts — see `context/source/cpss-structure.md`).
> Module *shape* was proposed before the PDFs were readable and held up; every module

Eleven modules across four blocks. An intern works through them individually — **there
is no cohort, so this is a sequence, not a schedule.** Someone arriving in week six
starts at Module 1 while the current intern is on Module 8. That is fine and is the
point.

---

## The format — read this before the module list

The single most important design decision here, and the one most likely to be
overridden by instinct.

**A module is not a PowerPoint Eric builds.** Clemson can run a deck-per-module program
because Clemson has staff. Applied Performance is one person with no protected time —
and the evidence is already in: the staff education series produced three decks and
stopped. Eleven intern decks would stop faster.

So each module is:

| Part | Who does the work | Time cost to Eric |
|---|---|---|
| **Read** — a section of the CPSS text | Intern | zero |
| **Do** — a task against our real data | Intern | zero once specified |
| **Discuss** — 20 minutes, no slides | Both | 20 min |
| **Evidence** — what it demonstrates | Intern produces, Eric signs | minutes |

**The task is the module.** Reading without doing produces someone who can discuss
monitoring and cannot run it. The discussion exists to catch misunderstanding, not to
transmit content — the text already did that.

**Slides accumulate rather than being built up front.** When a module's discussion has
happened three or four times and the same explanation keeps recurring, that explanation
is worth a deck — and by then it writes itself. Building eleven decks in advance is how
this dies in March.

---

## Block 1 · Foundations

Prerequisites for everything after. Do not reorder these.

### M1 — What Applied Performance is, and is not

**Read:** Ch1 Performance Dimensions · Ch30 Interdisciplinary Support
**CPSS:** Part 1 (role and scope), Part 7 · **Assessed:** RTP L1, COM L1

The role, and its edges. Who decides what. Applied Performance supplies evidence; it
does not clear athletes, prescribe fueling, or interpret psychological state.

- **Do:** Sit in on one cross-functional conversation. Afterwards, write down each
  decision made and who owned it.
- **Evidence:** Can state where AP's remit stops in three specific situations.
- **Why first:** An intern who blurs these boundaries in week two creates a problem no
  competency makes up for.

### M2 — Every measure has error

**Read:** Ch8 Data Hygiene
**CPSS:** Part 3 · **Assessed:** DL L2 · **Reference:**
`context/measurement-standards.md`

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.3.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
design, and get your human partner's approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
the approval gate never does.
</HARD-GATE>

## Three Paths

Before your first question, classify the request and say the
classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
override it:

- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
  built stays labeled throwaway.
- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
  questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
  sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
  starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
  bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
  one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.

When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.

## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"

Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
artifact, never the approval.

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |

## Checklist

Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
your path and complete them in order.

**Spike:**
1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway

**Bounded:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

**Architectural:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
    "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
    "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
    "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
```

**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
reported recommendation.

## The Process

The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
is the whole process.

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design (architectural path)

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:

# Baylor Sport Science — internship curriculum

The **content** of the Applied Performance internship program: what an intern reads,
what they do, and how they are assessed. Split out of `AgentAssist` on 2026-08-18.

```
modules.md    eleven modules in four blocks — the sequence an intern works through
handbook.md   the intern-facing handbook, written in second person
cpss-text/    the NSCA CPSS source material and the structural notes taken from it
              (PDFs and PPTXs are gitignored — purchased material, never pushed)
```

## The split, and why

`AgentAssist` is the **machine** — the question ledger, the agents, the deterministic
tools, the competency taxonomy, the education log. This repo is the **content** those
agents plan against. Keeping them apart means curriculum edits do not churn the plugin,
and plugin edits do not churn the curriculum.

The line:

| Lives here | Lives in `AgentAssist` |
|---|---|
| Module list, readings, tasks, evidence | `context/competencies.md` — the eight domain codes |
| Intern handbook | `context/department.md` — department facts |
| CPSS source material and chapter map | `context/measurement-standards.md` — the analytical spine |
| | `docs/education-log.md` — sessions actually delivered |
| | `agents/curriculum-architect.md` — the agent that edits this repo |

Paths written as `AgentAssist/...` in these files point at the sibling repo at
`~/DEV/AgentAssist`.

## The one design decision to preserve

**A module is not a PowerPoint Eric builds.** Applied Performance is one person with no
protected time. The staff deck series produced three decks and stopped; eleven intern
decks would stop faster. So the intern does the reading and the task, and the twenty
minutes of discussion is the only cost to Eric.

Slides accumulate rather than being built up front. When the same explanation has come
up in discussion three or four times, *then* it is worth a deck — and by then it writes
itself. See `modules.md` for the full statement of this.

## Status

Draft v1, 2026-08-18. Reading assignments are filled from the real CPSS chapter list
(31 chapters across 7 Parts). **Chapter assignments are proposed, not signed off** —
Eric picks the final set.

## Not CPSS exam preparation

Deliberate scope choice, not a gap. The text is a content spine and a standing
reference. Nobody here is optimising for someone sitting the exam.

# CLAUDE.md

Guidance for Claude Code when working in this repository.

## What this is

Curriculum **content** for the Baylor Athletics Applied Performance internship. Prose
and doctrine only — there is no code here. Split out of `~/DEV/AgentAssist` on
2026-08-18 so that curriculum edits and plugin edits stop churning each other.

Read `README.md` first for the layout and the split.

## The sibling repo

`~/DEV/AgentAssist` owns the machine: the question ledger, the agents, the
deterministic `tools/` layer, and the competency taxonomy. Paths written as
`AgentAssist/context/competencies.md` refer to that repo, not this one.

Two files there are load-bearing for anything written here:

- `AgentAssist/context/competencies.md` — the eight domain codes (`AM`, `NM`, `SP`,
  `DL`, `RTP`, `COM`, `RM`, `OPS`). Every module tags against these. **Renaming a code
  is a breaking change** across both repos — grep before editing.
- `AgentAssist/context/department.md` — department facts, including `<!-- TODO -->`
  markers for things only the department can supply. Flag a blocking TODO rather than
  substituting a plausible value.

The agent that edits this repo is `AgentAssist/agents/curriculum-architect.md`.

## Rules that survive the split

**Keep the program lean.** Applied Performance is one person covering every sport with
1–2 rolling interns. Anything that costs Eric keyboard time is a tax on the whole
department. A module that requires him to build something is a module that will not run.

**A module is not a deck.** The intern reads and does; the discussion is twenty minutes
with no slides. Slides accumulate from repeated discussions — they are never built up
front. If you find yourself proposing eleven decks, you have reproduced the failure
mode this design exists to avoid.

**There is no cohort.** Modules are a sequence, not a schedule. Someone arriving in week
six starts at Module 1 while the current intern is on Module 8. Do not add dates,
weeks, or cohort language.

**Chapter assignments are proposed, not signed off.** Eric picks the final set. Do not
present them as settled.

**This is not CPSS exam preparation.** Follow the text's themes; do not optimise for the
exam.

## Athlete data

Student-athlete data is FERPA-covered, possibly HIPAA-covered, and is **not** covered by
Baylor's AI approval. Nothing identifiable enters a prompt or a file in this repo.
Module tasks that touch real data are run by the intern against the local tools in
`AgentAssist/tools/`, and only de-identified or aggregate results are written up.

## Source material

`cpss-text/*.pdf` and `*.pptx` are purchased NSCA material and a colleague's decks.
**Gitignored — never commit them.** Re-copy from
`~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-BaylorUniversity/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/09_PRO_DEV/Courses/CPSS/`
if you need them on another machine.

`cpss-text/cpss-structure.md` is the tracked distillation: the real chapter list, the
CPSS-Part-to-domain map, and the corrections made when the PDFs were finally read.
Where it is marked as verified against the real materials, do not re-guess it.

present them as settled.

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## What this repository is

A **Claude Code plugin** for the Baylor Athletics Applied Performance department,
built on the WAT pattern (Workflows, Agents, Tools). Most of it is prompts, domain
doctrine, and a plain-text ledger; the `tools/` layer is real Python.

The governing principle, and the one to preserve when editing: **probabilistic AI
handles reasoning, deterministic code handles execution.** If a step has one correct
answer — a date stamp, a sequential ID, a standard deviation, a count — it belongs in
`tools/`, not in a prompt. Agents that reimplement tool work in prose are a
regression, even when the prose looks right.

## Layout

```
workflows/   markdown SOPs — objective, inputs, tools, steps, outputs, edge cases
agents/      roles and judgement — which workflow, what "done" means
tools/       deterministic Python, stdlib except archive.py --db
             ledger.py  capture/parse/IDs · reliability.py  TE, SWC, verdicts
             archive.py GPS archive audit  · check.py  the verification gate
commands/    slash-command entry points
context/     domain doctrine the agents load
ledger/      the question ledger (inbox + backlog)
docs/        education log, generated research briefs
```

## Athlete data: the tools layer is a privacy boundary

Baylor's approved AI path covers general use but does **not** address student-athlete
data. Until someone rules explicitly, athlete data is unapproved rather than
permitted-by-default (FERPA, possibly HIPAA).

This lands cleanly on the existing split, and it is the most useful consequence of
having a tools layer at all:

| Layer | Athlete data |
|---|---|
| `tools/` — deterministic Python, runs locally, no model involved | **Yes** |
| Agents and prompts | **No** — de-identified or aggregate only |

So automation of athlete data is not forbidden; it is `tools/` work. A wrangling script
that joins Catapult exports to ForceDecks output is fine. Pasting the resulting roster
into a prompt is not. When a question genuinely needs identifiable data in a prompt,
flag it and get a ruling rather than proceeding carefully.

## Verification — the definition of done

```bash
python3 tools/check.py
```

**Clean exit is the definition of done.** Any agent that writes to `ledger/`,
`docs/research/`, `agents/`, or `commands/` must run this before reporting finished
work, and must fix what it reports rather than explaining it away.

This follows Boris Cherny's rule — *give the agent a way to verify its work and quality
goes up 2–3×; build the verification, not the prompt.* It is why `check.py` exists as
a gate rather than as advice.

What it catches: duplicate or gapped Q-numbers, off-taxonomy routes/domains/statuses,
entries routed but never sharpened, PARK without a reason, missing required fields,
inbox lines that no longer parse (silently un-triageable captures), agent frontmatter
whose `name` disagrees with its filename, markdown references to files that do not
exist, tools that do not compile, and research briefs missing required sections.

Suites run individually: `check.py ledger`, `check.py plugin`, `check.py briefs`.

Warnings never fail the run; errors exit 1.

## Architecture

One ledger feeding three producers, tied together by a competency taxonomy.

```
ledger/inbox.md ──/triage──> question-triage ──> ledger/backlog.md
                                                  │
                            ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
                        TEACH                  STUDY                 ANSWER
                            │                     │                     │
                   education-planner      research-designer   analytics-feasibility
                            │                     │
                   five-slides-generator   docs/research/
                     (external skill)
                            └──────── curriculum-architect ────────┘
```

**`context/competencies.md` is the keystone.** Eight domain codes (`AM`, `NM`, `SP`,
`DL`, `RTP`, `COM`, `RM`, `OPS`) are the shared index across triage tagging,
education planning, and internship targets. Changing or renaming a domain code is a
breaking change — every agent references these codes and several files tabulate them.
Grep for the code before editing.

**`context/department.md` is load-bearing and incomplete.** It carries `<!-- TODO -->`
markers for facts only the department can supply (vendors, roster sizes, calendar
dates, compliance contacts). Agents are instructed to flag a blocking TODO rather than
substitute a plausible value. Preserve that instruction when editing agents — a
guessed fact about whether the AMS joins to GPS produces confidently wrong feasibility
calls downstream.

**`context/measurement-standards.md` is the analytical spine.** It encodes the ordering
rule that `analytics-feasibility` and `research-designer` must follow: establish the
noise floor (typical error vs. smallest worthwhile change) *before* assessing whether
a change is meaningful. This ordering is deliberately restated in both agents because
skipping to "is it meaningful" is the default behavior of both humans and LLMs.

## The inbox/backlog split

Two files with deliberately different friction, and the split is the core design bet:

- `ledger/inbox.md` — one line, no categories, no dedup, no cleanup. `/capture` must
  stay this cheap or people stop using it on a practice field.
- `ledger/backlog.md` — structured blocks with route, domain, feasibility, effort,
  `asked-count`.

Do **not** add validation, categorization, or duplicate-checking to `/capture`. Every
one of those is a reason to skip capturing, and the whole system dies at that step.
Duplicates are intentional signal — `asked-count` is the primary priority metric.

Entries are *moved* from inbox to backlog by triage, never deleted.

## Adding to the plugin

Decide the layer first:

| The thing is… | Goes in |
|---|---|
| A repeatable procedure with defined inputs and outputs | `workflows/` |
| Judgement, role, or "what done means" | `agents/` |
| Deterministic — one correct answer every time | `tools/` |
| A user entry point | `commands/` |
| Domain fact or doctrine | `context/` |

- **Agents** → `agents/<name>.md`, YAML frontmatter with `name`, `description`,
  `tools`. The `description` routes work to the agent, so write it as trigger
  conditions, not a job title.
- **Commands** → `commands/<name>.md`, frontmatter with `description`,
  `argument-hint`, `allowed-tools`. `$ARGUMENTS` interpolates user input.
- **Tools** → stdlib Python with an `argparse` CLI and JSON or plain-text output, so

## Load first

- `docs/education-log.md` — what staff education they will receive alongside

## The shape of this particular program

Before designing anything, internalize the actual constraints from
`context/department.md`:

- **Eric is the entire full-time department.** Supervision capacity is one person's
  attention, and that person also covers every sport.
- **1–2 interns, rolling starts.** There is no cohort. Onboarding cannot assume peers
  starting together, and there is no cohort-wide teaching moment to lean on.
- **Data wrangling is the department's biggest time sink.**

What follows from that: **keep the program lean.** A handbook, a rubric set, and a
milestone schedule designed for a ten-intern cohort is overhead that will not be
maintained, and an unmaintained program is worse than a simple one. Design something a
solo supervisor can actually run in the margins of a full workload.

Two things this constraint makes *more* valuable, not less:

- **An intern who reduces the wrangling load pays for their own supervision.** OPS
  competency is not the unglamorous option here; it is the one with the clearest return
  for the department.
- **Capture is a week-one responsibility.** With no other staff, interns are the only
  second source of questions in the ledger, and it doubles as an RM/DL rep.

## Program architecture

### Competency targets, not hour counts
An intern's plan is a **target level per domain plus the evidence that proves it**.
Never a list of hours served. "Completed 200 hours" describes attendance; "reached L3
in AM, demonstrated by independently producing four weekly football load reports the
coach used" describes a practitioner.

Realistic one-semester target: **L3 in two or three domains, L1–L2 across the rest.**
Depth in a few beats a shallow pass over eight. Interns and their universities will
push for breadth; resist it. Breadth without depth produces someone who can name
things and do none of them.

### Rotations
Structure exposure so every intern touches multiple sports and multiple data streams,
but anchor them to one primary sport for continuity. The relationship with one
coaching staff over a full term teaches things no rotation schedule can — most of
COM, in fact.

### Weekly rhythm
A defensible week has four parts:

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Delivery** | Recurring owned responsibility — the Monday report, the Tuesday testing block. Reliability is a competency. |
| **Supervised practice** | New skills with a staff member watching. This is where L1 becomes L2. |
| **Education** | Attend staff sessions; later in term, *deliver* one. |
| **Project** | One ledger-derived piece of work they own end to end. |

The delivery component is where interns learn that being depended upon is the job.
Protect it — do not let project work eat it.

### The intern presents
Every intern delivers at least one education session to cross-functional staff before
they leave. Non-negotiable. COM is the domain that determines whether they get hired,
and it is the one nearly every internship under-trains because it is uncomfortable to
supervise. Schedule it early enough that they get a second attempt.

### Projects come from the ledger
Pull from `ledger/backlog.md`, filtered to intern-suitable scope. A real question
someone actually asked, with a real deliverable, beats an invented exercise —
interns can tell the difference immediately and it changes how hard they work.

Scope to their tenure. A semester intern owns a discrete piece of a season-long
project, not the whole thing. Define the piece precisely and define what "done" is on
day one.

Behavioral evidence per competency, not impressions. For each target domain:

```
DOMAIN · target level
  EVIDENCE REQUIRED   the specific observable thing they must do
  OBSERVED BY         who signs off
  CHECKPOINT          when
```

tick it. "Independently produced the weekly load report for four consecutive weeks

Worked Example: Post-Practice Cognitive Deficit
Platform: LinkedIn
We schedule team meetings right after practice because everyone’s there.
Logistically, it makes sense. Physiologically, it’s the worst possible window.
After intense physical exertion, the brain prioritizes homeostasis and motor memory consolidation. Executive functions—working memory, processing speed, attention—are compromised. Fluid balance is off. Glucose is depleted. The athlete is physically present but cognitively checked out.
That “life skills” session or academic briefing you just delivered? Retention is near zero.
The fix isn’t complicated: build a 60–90-minute transition buffer between practice and any educational content that requires actual learning. Use that post-practice window for logistics only—bus times, schedule changes, quick reminders. Save the real content for when the brain is ready to receive it.
What does your post-practice window look like? Are you delivering content when athletes can absorb it?

# Education Content Agent

Turns a topic and an angle into finished education content for Baylor Athletics
Applied Performance — a researched, sourced brief, then a "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" deck
and a printed one-pager built from it.

```
topic + your angle
        │
        ▼
  content-researcher ──> briefs/YYYY-MM-DD-slug.md    a sourced fact sheet, no slides
        │
        ▼
  content-writer ──┬──> deck outline  ──> five-slides-generator skill ──> .pptx
                   └──> one-pager     ──> html-to-pdf skill           ──> .pdf
```

## Why this exists

Applied Performance is one person. The staff deck series stalled, and it stalled at the
expensive step: researching a topic properly and writing it into a narrative. Building
the `.pptx` was never the bottleneck — a skill already does that.

So this project takes the expensive step. It does **not** build slides.

## Layout

```
context/house-style.md   the house formats, transcribed from the department's own
                         templates — deck, social post, video script, one-pager
topics/library.md        the 30-topic library, 6 categories, with build status
briefs/                  the fact-sheet library — one file per topic, permanent
agents/                  content-researcher, content-writer
commands/                /brief, /deck, /onepager
tools/                   new_brief.py (scaffold), check.py (the gate)
```

## Quick start

```bash
# 1. start a brief for a topic
python3 tools/new_brief.py "Cold Exposure Timing"

# 2. in Claude Code, research it
/brief Cold Exposure Timing

# 3. turn the brief into a deck, or a one-pager, or both
/deck Cold Exposure Timing
/onepager Cold Exposure Timing

# 4. verify before you call it done
python3 tools/check.py
```

## The rule that keeps this project honest

**Research once, publish many.** A brief is written once and reused for every format.
If a topic is being researched a second time, the first brief was not good enough —
improve it rather than starting over.

## What it will not do

It does not write the `.pptx` and it does not lay out the PDF. Those belong to the
`five-slides-generator` and `html-to-pdf` skills, which already exist and already carry
the brand. Rebuilding either is a regression — see `CLAUDE.md`.

## Related

- `~/DEV/AgentAssist` — the question ledger and the agents that decide *what* to teach.
  `agents/education-planner.md` there picks the topic; this project makes the content.
- `~/DEV/CPSS_BaylorSportScience_Curriculum` — the intern curriculum content.
- `~/DEV/TechEd_Prop` — prior education artifacts, including the Baylor brand CSS and
  the ShiftWave protocol card that the one-pager format is derived from.

# CLAUDE.md

Guidance for Claude Code when working in this repository.

## What this is

A content engine for Baylor Athletics Applied Performance staff education. A topic and
an angle go in; a sourced brief comes out; formatted content is written from that brief.

Read `README.md` for the layout, then `context/house-style.md` before writing any
content. The house style is not a suggestion — it was written by the department and the
existing decks follow it.

## The boundary that defines this project

**This project researches and writes. It does not render.**

| Step | Owner |
|---|---|
| Research the topic, source every claim | `agents/content-researcher.md` here |
| Write the narrative into house format | `agents/content-writer.md` here |
| Build the `.pptx` | `five-slides-generator` skill |
| Build the printed PDF | `html-to-pdf` skill + the Baylor CSS in `~/DEV/TechEd_Prop` |

Reuse beats rebuild. AgentAssist once grew a CSV parser that was a worse copy of a
pipeline that already existed, and deleting it was the right call. A pptxgenjs builder
in this repo would be the same mistake. If a rendering step is missing something, fix
the skill, not this repo.

## Research standards

**Every number in a deck comes from a source.** Not from recall, not from a plausible
figure. A brief with an unsourced claim is not finished.

Search order, and it matters:

1. **The user's Zotero library first** — via the `sports-science-research-grounding`
   skill. Content that cites papers Eric already owns is content he can defend in a
   room, and he can pull the full text in seconds.
2. **Peer-reviewed external sources** second, clearly labelled as outside the library.
3. **Practitioner sources** (position stands, elite-program practice) third, and named
   as practice rather than evidence.

Where the evidence is genuinely thin or contested, **say so in the brief**. A slide that
presents a contested finding as settled is worse than no slide.

## Doctrine this content must respect

Carried over from `~/DEV/AgentAssist/CLAUDE.md`, because content that violates it
teaches the department the wrong thing:

- **ACWR is contested, not settled.** An ACWR deck already exists in the examples.
  Anything written here about workload ratios states the criticism, not just the method.
  Presenting ACWR as established practice is a competency failure, not a simplification.
- **Establish the noise floor before claiming a change is meaningful.** Typical error
  and smallest worthwhile change come first; "is this change real" comes second. This
  is the ordering both humans and language models skip by default.
- **Return-to-play clearance is a medical decision.** Applied Performance supplies
  evidence. No content phrases anything as a clearance recommendation.
- **Prefer within-athlete framing.** Squad sizes make between-athlete comparison
  fragile; each athlete as their own control is the applied setting's advantage.

## Athlete data

Student-athlete data is FERPA-covered, possibly HIPAA-covered, and is **not** covered by
Baylor's AI approval. Education content is general or aggregate by nature, so this
should never come up — and that is the point. **No identifiable athlete data enters a
brief, a deck, a one-pager, or a prompt in this repo.** If a topic seems to need a real
athlete example, use a composite and label it as one.

## Every deck corrects a misconception

Taken from `AgentAssist/agents/education-planner.md`, and it is the single most useful
constraint here. Additive-only sessions are forgotten by Friday. Before writing, you
must be able to fill in both:

- **THE ONE THING** — the sentence they should still know in a month.
- **THE MISCONCEPTION** — what they currently believe that is wrong.

If you cannot write the misconception, the topic is not ready. Say so rather than
writing a deck that only adds facts.

## Verification — the definition of done

```bash
python3 tools/check.py
```

Clean exit is the definition of done. Anything that writes to `briefs/` or
`topics/library.md` runs this before reporting finished work, and fixes what it reports
rather than explaining it away.

## Adding to this repo

| The thing is… | Goes in |
|---|---|
| A house format or a standard | `context/` |
| Judgement — what "good" means for a role | `agents/` |
| A user entry point | `commands/` |
| Deterministic — one right answer every time | `tools/` |
| Researched material about one topic | `briefs/` |

Tools are stdlib Python with an `argparse` CLI, so they run with no setup step.

# House style

The department's own formats. Slide arc, timings, and standards below are transcribed
from `5_Sides_Content_Templates.docx` in
`~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-BaylorUniversity/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/07_EDUCATION/5slides5minutes/`
— that document is the primary source. Where this file and that document disagree, the
document wins and this file is wrong.

Four formats. **Two are wired to commands today** (deck, one-pager). Two are
transcribed and ready but not yet wired (social post, video script).

---

## The production order

From the source document, and worth keeping:

| Step | Action | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Build the 5-slide deck | Forces the core idea, the structure, and the takeaway. This is the foundation. |
| 2 | Write the social post | Distils the deck to its sharpest form. If it will not fit in 200 words, the deck needs work. |
| 3 | Script the video | The social post becomes the outline; adapt for spoken delivery. |

The one-pager slots in after step 1 for the same reason — it is the deck with the
talking points folded in, for a room you will not be standing in.

---

## Format 1 — the 5-slide deck  *(wired: `/deck`)*

### Standards

| Element | Standard |
|---|---|
| Duration | 5 minutes. Hard ceiling 7 minutes with Q&A. |
| Slides | **Exactly 5. No exceptions.** The constraint drives the clarity. |
| Audience | Cross-functional H&W staff — S&C, Athletic Medicine, Sport Science, Nutrition, Mental Health |
| Tone | Practitioner sharing with peers. Confident, accessible, not academic. |
| Depth | Surface-level *by design*. The goal is awareness plus one takeaway, not mastery. |
| Outcome | Spark curiosity. Ideally leads to a longer conversation or a full Performance School session. |

### The arc

| Slide | Time | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~45 sec | **THE HOOK** — title plus an opening question or scenario. Why should a room of diverse practitioners care? Make it cross-functional. |
| 2 | ~60 sec | **THE PROBLEM / CONTEXT** — the gap, misconception, or missed opportunity. A stat, a common scenario, or "what we typically see." Ground it in their daily reality. |
| 3 | ~75 sec | **THE INSIGHT** — the core concept. One big idea, clearly explained. A visual, analogy, or data point that sticks. No jargon that fails to cross disciplines. |
| 4 | ~60 sec | **THE APPLICATION** — so what? How it shows up across specialties. One or two examples, or "what this looks like on Monday." |
| 5 | ~45 sec | **THE TAKEAWAY** — one actionable thing. End with a question that invites the longer conversation. |

Backgrounds alternate **dark, light, dark, light, dark**. This is the visual signature
of the series; the `five-slides-generator` skill enforces it. Never break it.

### What to hand off

The `five-slides-generator` skill builds the `.pptx`. Give it, per slide: slide content
(the words on the slide) and talking points (what is said out loud). Plus:

```
TOPIC
CATEGORY            from topics/library.md
PRESENTER
CORE QUESTION       the one question this talk answers
THE ONE THING       the sentence they still know in a month
THE MISCONCEPTION   what they currently believe that is wrong
FOLLOW-UP POTENTIAL could this become a full Performance School session?
```

Its house rule, worth restating: *if you cannot explain the core idea in one sentence,
you are not ready to present it.* Scratch the surface on purpose — depth comes in the
follow-up conversation.

---

## Format 2 — the one-pager  *(wired: `/onepager`)*

**New format.** There is no template for it in the source document, so this is derived
from the deck arc and from the ShiftWave protocol card in
`~/DEV/TechEd_Prop/ShitfWave/` — the department's existing printed-artifact precedent.

### Standards

| Element | Standard |
|---|---|
| Size | One page, US Letter portrait. One page is the whole constraint. |
| Purpose | The deck for a room you are not standing in. Left on a desk, pinned in a training room, handed to a coach. |
| Audience | Same cross-functional staff, reading alone with no presenter |
| Tone | Same practitioner voice. Slightly more complete, because nobody is there to answer a question. |
| Brand | `~/DEV/TechEd_Prop/ShitfWave/baylor-brand.css` |
| Build | HTML, then the `html-to-pdf` skill. Never hand-laid-out. |

### The blocks

| Block | Content |
|---|---|
| Title + core question | The topic, and the one question this answers |
| The problem | Two to three sentences. The gap or misconception, grounded in their day. |
| The insight | The core concept, plus **one** visual. This is the block a reader remembers. |
| On Monday | Two or three concrete lines, split by specialty where that helps |
| The one thing | A single boxed sentence — the takeaway, quotable |
| Sources | Three to five, so the reader can check the work |
| Who to ask | Name and role, so a question has somewhere to go |

**Differences from the deck, deliberate:** sources are printed (a deck cites verbally),
and there is no discussion prompt (nobody is in the room), replaced by a contact line.

---

## Format 3 — the social post  *(transcribed, not yet wired)*

| Element | Standard |
|---|---|
| Platform | LinkedIn (long-form) or X (short-form) |
| Length | LinkedIn 150–250 words · X 280 characters, or a 3–5 post thread |
| Tone | Conversational, credible, practitioner-to-practitioner. Not academic, not salesy. |
| Structure | Hook → Insight → Takeaway → Engagement prompt |
| Visuals | Optional — one graphic, infographic, or quote card |
| Hashtags | 2–4 relevant tags |

| Section | Length | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Hook | 1–2 sentences | Stop the scroll. Question, surprising stat, or contrarian take. |
| Insight | 3–5 sentences | One concept explained clearly, with evidence or experience. |
| Takeaway | 1–2 sentences | One practical thing to do or think about differently. |
| Engage | 1 sentence | A question that invites practitioners to share their experience. |

Audience is **external** — peers and industry, not internal staff. Goal is thought
leadership and visibility.

---

## Format 4 — the video script  *(transcribed, not yet wired)*

| Element | Standard |
|---|---|
| Duration | 60–90 seconds. Hard ceiling 2 minutes. |
| Tone | Direct, conversational, confident. Talk to camera like a colleague, not a lecturer. |
| Format | Direct-to-camera, optional text overlays or simple graphics |
| Captions | Always. Most social video is watched with the sound off. |
| CTA | Every video ends with one clear takeaway or follow prompt. |

| Section | Time | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Hook | 5–10 sec | Bold statement or question. Land it in the first 3 seconds. |
| The Problem | 10–15 sec | The common mistake or misconception. Make the viewer feel seen. |
| The Insight | 20–30 sec | One concept, clearly explained. A stat or analogy if it helps. |
| The Fix | 15–20 sec | One practical action. "Try this tomorrow." |
| Close | 5–10 sec | Reinforce the point, then the prompt. |

House rule from the source: *write the way you talk. Read it out loud before filming.
If it sounds like a script, rewrite it until it sounds like you explaining something to
a colleague over coffee.*

---

## One topic, four formats

| | Social | Video | Deck | One-pager |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Audience** | External peers | External + internal | Internal H&W staff | Internal, reading alone |
| **Length** | 150–250 words | 60–90 sec | 5 min, 5 slides | 1 page |
| **Depth** | One insight + one takeaway | Problem → insight → fix | Hook → problem → insight → application → takeaway | Deck, plus sources |
| **Goal** | Thought leadership | Awareness, shareability | Spark curiosity | Reference after the room empties |

The core idea never changes across formats. Depth, length, and audience do. All four are
written from the **same brief** — see `briefs/README.md`.

---

## Where the rendering lives

# House style

The department's own formats. Slide arc, timings, and standards below are transcribed
from `5_Sides_Content_Templates.docx` in
`~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-BaylorUniversity/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/07_EDUCATION/5slides5minutes/`
— that document is the primary source. Where this file and that document disagree, the
document wins and this file is wrong.

Four formats. **Two are wired to commands today** (deck, one-pager). Two are
transcribed and ready but not yet wired (social post, video script).

---

## The production order

From the source document, and worth keeping:

| Step | Action | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Build the 5-slide deck | Forces the core idea, the structure, and the takeaway. This is the foundation. |
| 2 | Write the social post | Distils the deck to its sharpest form. If it will not fit in 200 words, the deck needs work. |
| 3 | Script the video | The social post becomes the outline; adapt for spoken delivery. |

The one-pager slots in after step 1 for the same reason — it is the deck with the
talking points folded in, for a room you will not be standing in.

---

## Format 1 — the 5-slide deck  *(wired: `/deck`)*

### Standards

| Element | Standard |
|---|---|
| Duration | 5 minutes. Hard ceiling 7 minutes with Q&A. |
| Slides | **Exactly 5. No exceptions.** The constraint drives the clarity. |
| Audience | Cross-functional H&W staff — S&C, Athletic Medicine, Sport Science, Nutrition, Mental Health |
| Tone | Practitioner sharing with peers. Confident, accessible, not academic. |
| Depth | Surface-level *by design*. The goal is awareness plus one takeaway, not mastery. |
| Outcome | Spark curiosity. Ideally leads to a longer conversation or a full Performance School session. |

### The arc

| Slide | Time | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~45 sec | **THE HOOK** — title plus an opening question or scenario. Why should a room of diverse practitioners care? Make it cross-functional. |
| 2 | ~60 sec | **THE PROBLEM / CONTEXT** — the gap, misconception, or missed opportunity. A stat, a common scenario, or "what we typically see." Ground it in their daily reality. |
| 3 | ~75 sec | **THE INSIGHT** — the core concept. One big idea, clearly explained. A visual, analogy, or data point that sticks. No jargon that fails to cross disciplines. |
| 4 | ~60 sec | **THE APPLICATION** — so what? How it shows up across specialties. One or two examples, or "what this looks like on Monday." |
| 5 | ~45 sec | **THE TAKEAWAY** — one actionable thing. End with a question that invites the longer conversation. |

Backgrounds alternate **dark, light, dark, light, dark**. This is the visual signature
of the series; the `five-slides-generator` skill enforces it. Never break it.

### What to hand off

The `five-slides-generator` skill builds the `.pptx`. Give it, per slide: slide content
(the words on the slide) and talking points (what is said out loud). Plus:

```
TOPIC
CATEGORY            from topics/library.md
PRESENTER
CORE QUESTION       the one question this talk answers
THE ONE THING       the sentence they still know in a month
THE MISCONCEPTION   what they currently believe that is wrong
FOLLOW-UP POTENTIAL could this become a full Performance School session?
```

Its house rule, worth restating: *if you cannot explain the core idea in one sentence,
you are not ready to present it.* Scratch the surface on purpose — depth comes in the
follow-up conversation.

---

## Format 2 — the one-pager  *(wired: `/onepager`)*

**New format.** There is no template for it in the source document, so this is derived
from the deck arc and from the ShiftWave protocol card in
`~/DEV/TechEd_Prop/ShitfWave/` — the department's existing printed-artifact precedent.

### Standards

| Element | Standard |
|---|---|
| Size | One page, US Letter portrait. One page is the whole constraint. |
| Purpose | The deck for a room you are not standing in. Left on a desk, pinned in a training room, handed to a coach. |
| Audience | Same cross-functional staff, reading alone with no presenter |
| Tone | Same practitioner voice. Slightly more complete, because nobody is there to answer a question. |
| Brand | `~/DEV/TechEd_Prop/ShitfWave/baylor-brand.css` |
| Build | HTML, then the `html-to-pdf` skill. Never hand-laid-out. |

### The blocks

| Block | Content |
|---|---|
| Title + core question | The topic, and the one question this answers |
| The problem | Two to three sentences. The gap or misconception, grounded in their day. |
| The insight | The core concept, plus **one** visual. This is the block a reader remembers. |
| On Monday | Two or three concrete lines, split by specialty where that helps |
| The one thing | A single boxed sentence — the takeaway, quotable |
| Sources | Three to five, so the reader can check the work |
| Who to ask | Name and role, so a question has somewhere to go |

**Differences from the deck, deliberate:** sources are printed (a deck cites verbally),
and there is no discussion prompt (nobody is in the room), replaced by a contact line.

---

## Format 3 — the social post  *(transcribed, not yet wired)*

| Element | Standard |
|---|---|
| Platform | LinkedIn (long-form) or X (short-form) |
| Length | LinkedIn 150–250 words · X 280 characters, or a 3–5 post thread |
| Tone | Conversational, credible, practitioner-to-practitioner. Not academic, not salesy. |
| Structure | Hook → Insight → Takeaway → Engagement prompt |
| Visuals | Optional — one graphic, infographic, or quote card |
| Hashtags | 2–4 relevant tags |

| Section | Length | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Hook | 1–2 sentences | Stop the scroll. Question, surprising stat, or contrarian take. |
| Insight | 3–5 sentences | One concept explained clearly, with evidence or experience. |
| Takeaway | 1–2 sentences | One practical thing to do or think about differently. |
| Engage | 1 sentence | A question that invites practitioners to share their experience. |

Audience is **external** — peers and industry, not internal staff. Goal is thought
leadership and visibility.

---

## Format 4 — the video script  *(transcribed, not yet wired)*

| Element | Standard |
|---|---|
| Duration | 60–90 seconds. Hard ceiling 2 minutes. |
| Tone | Direct, conversational, confident. Talk to camera like a colleague, not a lecturer. |
| Format | Direct-to-camera, optional text overlays or simple graphics |
| Captions | Always. Most social video is watched with the sound off. |
| CTA | Every video ends with one clear takeaway or follow prompt. |

| Section | Time | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Hook | 5–10 sec | Bold statement or question. Land it in the first 3 seconds. |
| The Problem | 10–15 sec | The common mistake or misconception. Make the viewer feel seen. |
| The Insight | 20–30 sec | One concept, clearly explained. A stat or analogy if it helps. |
| The Fix | 15–20 sec | One practical action. "Try this tomorrow." |
| Close | 5–10 sec | Reinforce the point, then the prompt. |

House rule from the source: *write the way you talk. Read it out loud before filming.
If it sounds like a script, rewrite it until it sounds like you explaining something to
a colleague over coffee.*

---

## One topic, four formats

| | Social | Video | Deck | One-pager |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Audience** | External peers | External + internal | Internal H&W staff | Internal, reading alone |
| **Length** | 150–250 words | 60–90 sec | 5 min, 5 slides | 1 page |
| **Depth** | One insight + one takeaway | Problem → insight → fix | Hook → problem → insight → application → takeaway | Deck, plus sources |
| **Goal** | Thought leadership | Awareness, shareability | Spark curiosity | Reference after the room empties |

The core idea never changes across formats. Depth, length, and audience do. All four are
written from the **same brief** — see `briefs/README.md`.

---

## Where the rendering lives

  against the OneDrive originals.
- **One-pager** — the `html-to-pdf` skill, over HTML built with
  `~/DEV/TechEd_Prop/ShitfWave/baylor-brand.css`.

# Briefs

One file per topic. A brief is the researched, sourced substance of a topic — and
nothing else. **No slides, no layout, no format.** Every output format is written from
the brief, which is the whole point: research once, publish many.

## Naming

```
briefs/YYYY-MM-DD-slug.md
```

The date is the date research was done, so staleness is visible at a glance. Use
`tools/new_brief.py "Topic Name"` — it stamps the date and slug so they cannot drift.

## Required sections

`tools/check.py` fails the run if any of these are missing.

| Section | What goes in it |
|---|---|
| `## Core question` | The one question this topic answers. One sentence. |
| `## The one thing` | What they should still know in a month. One sentence. If you cannot write it, stop — the topic is not ready. |
| `## The misconception` | What they currently believe that is wrong. Every good session corrects something. |
| `## Findings` | 4–6 facts, each with a source. This is the substance. |
| `## What we do not know` | Where the evidence is thin, contested, or absent. Never empty — write "nothing material" only if that is true. |
| `## Application` | What this looks like on Monday, per specialty where it differs. |
| `## Anticipated pushback` | The two hardest questions and honest answers, including "we don't know." |
| `## Sources` | Numbered. Zotero items marked `[library]`. |

## Frontmatter

```yaml
---
topic: Cold Exposure Timing
library_id: 10          # number from topics/library.md, or "off-library"
category: Recovery & Load Management
researched: 2026-08-18
status: draft           # draft | ready
---
```

`status: ready` means the brief is good enough to write content from. Only a human sets
it.

## Sourcing rules

Every number carries a source. Zotero first, then peer-reviewed external, then
practitioner sources named as practice rather than evidence. The full rule is in
`CLAUDE.md` — read it before researching, not after.

## Reuse

If a topic already has a brief, **improve it rather than writing a second one.** Two
briefs on one topic means two versions of the truth, and the deck and the one-pager will
quietly disagree. Update `researched:` when you revise.

input.content:
---
name: content-researcher
description: Researches a staff-education topic and writes a sourced brief to briefs/ — findings, what we do not know, application, and anticipated pushback. Use before any deck, one-pager, social post, or video script is written, or when an existing brief is stale or thin. Does not write slides or layout.
tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, WebSearch, WebFetch, Bash
---

You research one topic and write one brief. You do not write slides, one-pagers, or any
formatted content — that is `content-writer`'s job, and it works from what you produce.

The value you add is not summary. Anyone can summarise. The value is that **every claim
in the finished content can be defended in a room full of specialists**, several of whom
know their own discipline better than the presenter does.

## Load first

- `CLAUDE.md` — the research standards and the doctrine the content must respect
- `briefs/README.md` — the required sections and the frontmatter
- `topics/library.md` — the topic's number, category, and current status
- Any existing brief on this topic. **Improve it rather than starting a second one.**

## Search order, and it matters

1. **The Zotero library first.** Use the `sports-science-research-grounding` skill.
   A finding that cites a paper Eric already owns is one he can pull up mid-question.
   Mark these `[library]` in the sources list.
2. **Peer-reviewed external** second. Label clearly as outside the library.
3. **Practitioner sources** third — position stands, what elite programs do. Name these
   as *practice*, not evidence. The difference is the whole point of the department.

## What a finding must have

Four to six findings. Each one:

- A specific claim, not a gesture at a literature
- The actual number where there is one
- A source, numbered into `## Sources`
- Where the finding is contested, the counter-position in the same breath

**A finding you cannot source does not go in the brief.** Not as a hedge, not as
"research suggests." Drop it, or go find the source.

## The sections that people skip, and must not

**`## What we do not know`.** This is the section that makes the department credible.
Sport science is full of confident claims about thin evidence, and a room of
practitioners can smell it. Write down where the evidence is weak, where the effect is
small, where the studies were done on a population that is not ours.

description: Turns a researched brief into house-format content — a 5-slide deck outline handed to the five-slides-generator skill, or a one-page HTML handout handed to html-to-pdf. Use after a brief exists. Never researches from scratch and never builds the .pptx or lays out the PDF itself.
tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash, Skill
---

You turn a brief into content someone can present or hand out. You do not research and
you do not render.

## The boundary, stated plainly

| You do | You do not |
|---|---|
| Write the narrative — the words on the slide and the words spoken | Write pptxgenjs code |
| Write the one-pager's HTML content against the existing brand CSS | Design a new layout or a new brand |
| Hand off to the skill that builds the artifact | Build the artifact |

`five-slides-generator` owns the `.pptx`. `html-to-pdf` owns the PDF. If a skill is
missing something you need, **fix the skill** — do not work around it here. A renderer
in this repo is the regression `CLAUDE.md` exists to prevent.

## Load first

- `context/house-style.md` — the arc, the timings, the standards. Non-negotiable.
- The brief in `briefs/`. **If there is no brief, stop and run `content-researcher`
  first.** Writing content from your own recall is exactly the failure this project
  exists to prevent.
- `CLAUDE.md` — the doctrine the content must respect.

## If the brief is not ready

Say so and stop. Specifically:

- `status: draft` and thin findings → it needs more research, not better writing.
- `## The misconception` empty → the topic is not ready. Additive-only content is
  forgotten by Friday. Report that rather than writing around it.
- `## What we do not know` empty → send it back. Nothing is that clean.

Writing polished content over a weak brief produces something that fails in the room,
and the failure lands on the presenter, not on you.

## Writing the deck

Five slides. Exactly five. The arc and the per-slide timing are in
`context/house-style.md` — follow them rather than restating them here.

For each slide produce two things, kept separate:

- **Slide content** — the words that appear. Few. A 5-minute deck that is read aloud
  from the slide has already failed.
- **Talking points** — what is said. This is where the substance lives.

Then hand the whole thing to the `five-slides-generator` skill, which owns the format,
the design constants, and the build.

Three things the room will punish:

- **Jargon that does not cross disciplines.** The audience is S&C, Athletic Medicine,
  Sport Science, Nutrition, and Mental Health at once. A term that only one of them uses
  loses the other four.
- **Depth.** Surface-level is the design, not a compromise. The goal is awareness plus
  one takeaway. Depth belongs in the follow-up conversation.
- **A takeaway that is not actionable.** Slide 5 asks for a specific behaviour, on
  Monday, by someone in that room.

## Writing the one-pager

Blocks and standards are in `context/house-style.md`. Build HTML against
`~/DEV/TechEd_Prop/ShitfWave/baylor-brand.css`, then hand it to the `html-to-pdf` skill.

Two differences from the deck, and they are deliberate:

- **Sources are printed.** A presenter cites verbally; a page cannot. Three to five.
- **No discussion prompt.** Nobody is in the room. Replace it with a name and a role, so
  a question has somewhere to go.

One page. If it does not fit, cut the content — never shrink the type.

## Doctrine, checked before you hand off

- Workload-ratio content **states the criticism of ACWR**. Presenting it as settled
  practice is a competency failure, not a simplification.
- Change-over-time content establishes the **noise floor first** — typical error and
  smallest worthwhile change — before claiming a change is meaningful. This ordering is
  the one both humans and language models skip by default.
- Nothing reads as a **return-to-play clearance recommendation**. Evidence only.
- Framing is **within-athlete** by preference.
- **No identifiable athlete data.** Composites, labelled as composites.

## Every number traces to the brief

Not to your recall, not to a plausible-looking figure. If a slide wants a number the
brief does not have, that is a research gap — send it back rather than filling it in.

## After the artifact exists

Update the topic's row in `topics/library.md` to `built`. When it has actually been
presented, the human marks it `delivered` here **and** records it in
`AgentAssist/docs/education-log.md`, including the "what didn't land" column — that
column is the only record of where a room got lost.

## Done means

```bash
python3 tools/check.py
```

Clean exit. Then report the artifact path, the one thing, and the misconception it
corrects — in that order, in three lines.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Scaffold a brief for a topic.

Stamps today's date and a slug so filenames cannot drift, and fills the frontmatter
from topics/library.md where the topic is found there. Everything a human would get
wrong by hand is done here; everything requiring judgement is left blank on purpose.

    python3 tools/new_brief.py "Cold Exposure Timing"
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import datetime as dt
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
BRIEFS = ROOT / "briefs"
LIBRARY = ROOT / "topics" / "library.md"

SECTIONS = [
    ("Core question", "The one question this topic answers. One sentence."),
    ("The one thing", "What they should still know in a month. One sentence.\n"
                      "If you cannot write it, the topic is not ready — say so."),
    ("The misconception", "What the room currently believes that is wrong.\n"
                          "Every good session corrects something, not just adds something."),
    ("Findings", "4-6 facts. Each one specific, each with a source number.\n"
                 "Where a finding is contested, the counter-position goes in the same breath."),
    ("What we do not know", "Where the evidence is thin, contested, or drawn from a\n"
                            "population that is not ours. Never leave this empty."),
    ("Application", "What this looks like on Monday, per specialty where it differs."),
    ("Anticipated pushback", "The two hardest questions and honest answers.\n"
                             "\"We don't know\" is acceptable and often correct."),
    ("Sources", "Numbered. Mark Zotero items [library]."),
]


def slugify(topic: str) -> str:
    s = topic.lower()
    s = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", s)
    return s.strip("-")


def lookup(topic: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Return (library_id, category) for a topic named in topics/library.md."""
    if not LIBRARY.exists():
        return "off-library", ""
    category = ""
    want = topic.strip().lower()
    for line in LIBRARY.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        if line.startswith("## "):
            category = line[3:].strip()
            continue
        cells = [c.strip() for c in line.split("|")]
        # a topic row is: | # | Topic | Hook | Status | Brief |
        if len(cells) >= 6 and cells[1].isdigit() and cells[2].lower() == want:
            return cells[1], category
    return "off-library", ""


def main() -> int:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__,
                                formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    p.add_argument("topic", help="topic name, ideally exactly as it appears in topics/library.md")
    p.add_argument("--date", default=None, help="override the research date (YYYY-MM-DD)")
    args = p.parse_args()

    date = args.date or dt.date.today().isoformat()
    slug = slugify(args.topic)
    if not slug:
        print("error: topic produced an empty slug", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    path = BRIEFS / f"{date}-{slug}.md"

    # A second brief on one topic means two versions of the truth, and the deck and the
    # one-pager will quietly disagree. Refuse rather than allow it.
    existing = sorted(BRIEFS.glob(f"*-{slug}.md"))
    if existing:
        print(f"a brief for this topic already exists: {existing[0].relative_to(ROOT)}")
        print("improve it rather than writing a second one.")
        return 1

    library_id, category = lookup(args.topic)

    body = [
        "---",
        f"topic: {args.topic}",
        f"library_id: {library_id}",
        f"category: {category}",
        f"researched: {date}",
        "status: draft",
        "---",
        "",
        f"# {args.topic}",
        "",
    ]
    for name, hint in SECTIONS:
        body.append(f"## {name}")
        body.append("")
        for line in hint.splitlines():
            body.append(f"<!-- {line} -->")
        body.append("")

    BRIEFS.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    path.write_text("\n".join(body), encoding="utf-8")
